prime.problem: The atom-by-atom BatchNorm backward takes a dozen lines and six throwaway gradient tensors, and without a short form you still need loss.backward() to train. You can't claim to understand the whole backward pass until you can write it all yourself and train on it.
prime.fits: The last step of the backprop-ninja lecture. It folds the twelve lines from the tanh-and-BatchNorm atoms card into one, the way the cross-entropy card folded the softmax chain into three, and then uses both short forms to train the BatchNorm MLP from makemore Part 3 with autograd switched off.
expect: the three roads from an input to the loss: direct, via the mean, via the variance
why dσ²/dμ = 0 when μ is the batch mean
the one-line dhprebn and its n/(n−1) factor
prime.goal: Derive and write the one-line BatchNorm backward, explain what each of its three terms is, and train the 12,297-parameter net to a validation loss near 2.11 without calling loss.backward().

attend: Each x<sub>i</sub> reaches the loss by three roads. Which term of the one-liner belongs to which road?
σ² is computed from μ, yet no gradient flows along that edge. What property of the batch mean makes the slope zero?
Which two sums in the one-liner are the same sums as dbnbias and dbngain, and why is that not a coincidence?
Why must each neuron's column of dhprebn sum to (nearly) zero?
Which part of the one-liner would change if the forward pass divided by n instead of n − 1, or used fixed running statistics?

must: μ and σ² are computed from all 32 inputs → each x<sub>i</sub> reaches the loss directly, via μ and via σ² → its gradient is the sum of three terms → the one-liner's n·dy<sub>i</sub>, −Σdy<sub>j</sub> and −n/(n−1)·x̂<sub>i</sub>·Σdy<sub>j</sub>x̂<sub>j</sub>
μ is the mean of the same values → Σ(x<sub>j</sub> − μ) = 0 → dσ²/dμ = 0 → the edge σ² → μ carries no gradient → the derivation collapses to one short broadcasted line

BatchNorm's output doesn't change if you shift, or (up to ε) scale, a neuron's whole batch → the gradient can't point along those directions → the one-liner removes the mean of dy and its component along x̂ → each column of dhprebn sums to ≈ 0 (5.6e-9 in the lab)

Every layer's gradient now has a short analytic form → the full backward pass is 14 lines → loss.backward() can be deleted and the loop wrapped in torch.no_grad() → the same training (val 2.1086 in the lab) with no autograd graph recorded
elevated: Roads ② and ③ reuse dhpreact.sum(0) and (dhpreact*bnraw).sum(0), the very sums that give dbnbias and dbngain → the short form costs little more than the parameter gradients you need anyway
The n/(n−1) factor comes from differentiating the ÷(n−1) variance → with a ÷n forward it must be 1 (keeping 32/31 fails cmp with maxdiff 3.9e-5 on the lab's batch)
reference: Exercise 4 uses n_hidden = 200: 12,297 parameters; lr 0.1 then 0.01 after step 100,000 of 200,000
grads = [dC, dW1, db1, dW2, db2, dbngain, dbnbias], applied with p.data += -lr * grad
BatchNorm is calibrated on the whole training set after training; the loop keeps no running statistics
measured: forward max diff 4.77e-7, one-liner maxdiff 9.31e-10, gradient checks 3.7e-9 to 1.5e-8, 200k steps in 126 s, train 2.0712 / val 2.1086 (notebook 2.0705 / 2.1099)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the BatchNorm graph for one neuron (x → μ, σ² → x̂ → y) and label the three roads from x<sub>i</sub> to the loss. Then write the one-liner and point to which term comes from which road, and say in one sentence why the σ² → μ edge contributes nothing.
checklist: three roads: direct, via μ, via σ²; the gradient is their sum
dσ²/dμ ∝ Σ(x<sub>j</sub> − μ) = 0 for the batch's own mean
the n/(n−1) comes from the ÷(n−1) variance
with every layer in short form, loss.backward() goes and training runs under no_grad

retrieve.q: Explain in plain words why the gradient of one BatchNorm input depends on the gradients of all 31 other rows in the batch.
answer: μ and σ² are computed from every row
so changing x<sub>i</sub> moves every x̂<sub>j</sub> through μ and σ²
those effects are weighed by each row's dy<sub>j</sub>, hence the sums over j

retrieve.q: Walk through the derivation in order: dx̂, then dσ², then dμ, then dx. What does each step multiply by, and where does a sum over j appear?
answer: dx̂<sub>i</sub> = γ·dy<sub>i</sub>
dσ² sums dx̂<sub>j</sub>·(x<sub>j</sub> − μ)·(−½)(σ² + ε)<sup>−3/2</sup> over j
dμ sums −s·dx̂<sub>j</sub> over j; the dσ²·dσ²/dμ part is 0
dx<sub>i</sub> adds s·dx̂<sub>i</sub>, dσ²·2(x<sub>i</sub> − μ)/(n − 1) and dμ/n

retrieve.q: Walk row 0 of neuron 0 through the one-liner: which three numbers go in the bracket, and what prefactor multiplies them?
answer: Σdyj = −0.00790285 (as dbnbias)
32/31 · x̂<sub>0</sub> · Σdy<sub>j</sub>x̂<sub>j</sub> = −0.00417372
bracket −0.0186301 × γs/n 0.0216354 = −0.000403071, matching autograd

retrieve.q: You need BatchNorm's backward for a production model. Would you write the one-liner, keep the atomic version, or rely on autograd? What does each cost you?
answer: autograd: no derivation, always consistent with the forward pass; you give up visibility, not correctness
one-liner: short and cheap, but tied to one exact forward (divisor, training vs inference) and only float-close to autograd
atomic: easy to check line by line, but many temporaries; best as the reference you test the one-liner against

compare.q: Both cards replace a chain of atomic lines with a short analytic form. What is structurally similar about softmax − one-hot and the BatchNorm bracket, and how can each go wrong?
answer: both rows/columns of the gradient sum to ≈ 0, because the output ignores a uniform shift of the inputs (logits in a row; a neuron's batch)
both need a paper derivation with careful indices, then cmp against autograd
both reach only approximate: True because the float operations are reordered
cross-entropy's form doesn't depend on a hyperparameter; BatchNorm's depends on the variance divisor

compare.q: The atomic card needs += for bndiff and hprebn; the one-liner has none. Where did those two-branch accumulations go?
answer: the += branches are the roads via μ and via σ²
in the one-liner they are the −Σdy and −n/(n−1)·x̂·Σdy·x̂ terms
the atomic version adds them tensor by tensor; the one-liner adds them inside one bracket

predict.q: Switch the net to evaluation: BatchNorm now uses fixed running statistics (bnmean, bnvar) instead of the batch's own. Which of the one-liner's three terms survive in the gradient with respect to hprebn, and would its columns still sum to zero?
predict.answer: Only road ① survives: μ and σ² are constants, so dx<sub>i</sub> = γ·s·dy<sub>i</sub>, one row at a time with no sums over the batch. The columns no longer sum to zero in general, because shifting the whole batch now does change every output: the fixed mean doesn't move with it.

apply.task: In your scratch copy of the lab, change the Exercise 3 forward pass to the ÷n variance (unbiased=False), recompute bnvar_inv and bnraw from it, backprop dhpreact through it with autograd, and cmp two versions of the one-liner: with the n/(n−1) factor and with 1. Before running, predict which one passes.
apply.done: The factor-1 version prints approximate: True | maxdiff: 9.313225746154785e-10 and the n/(n−1) version prints approximate: False | maxdiff: 3.902293974533677e-05 (my check run on the lab's seeded batch).
